stops.name: Hamilton, Ohio: the death of the prophet
stops.campa: Seriously ill, he comes home to Hamilton on the Great Miami, and there, on the twenty-ninth of May, John Cleves Symmes dies, forty-eight years old, six months short of forty-nine. He goes to his grave still pledging his life to the truth he never proved: the hollow earth, open at the poles, habitable within, the nested spheres turning unseen beneath the ice. The prophet is dead; the doctrine survives him in his son's keeping, and in the disciple's expedition already stirring toward the southern sea.

stops.name: Reynolds before Congress, the disciple's expedition
stops.campa: Seven years after the master's death, the disciple stands where the master's petitions fell. Jeremiah Reynolds delivers before the Congress his Address on a surveying and exploring expedition to the Pacific and the South Seas, and the words carry. From this agitation the nation at last fits out the United States Exploring Expedition, which sails in 1838 to chart the Antarctic verge. The polar voyage Symmes begged for is launched, sprung from his Circular, though it seeks an open sea where he sought a doorway to the world within.

stops.name: Hamilton, Ohio: the monument crowned with the hollow globe
stops.campa: At last the son does what the world would not: he raises the prophecy in stone. Americus Symmes erects over his father's grave in the old pioneer cemetery a square pedestal crowned with a carved globe: hollow, open at both poles, the earth as his father saw it. It is the only monument the hollow earth will ever have, and it still stands in Hamilton, Ohio. The doctrine that all the learned world derided is written now in stone, turning its open poles to the sky above the grave of the man who pledged his life to it.
stops.quote: The Earth is hollow, habitable within, and widely open about the poles.
stops.quote_source: Americus Symmes, Symmes's Theory of Concentric Spheres (1878), title compiled from his father's writings
